course_description:
The course provides students with an understanding of different theories of mass media systems, their philosophical foundations and basic principles. It looks at varying relationships of mass media to politics and society and their important role in social and political change. The media systems of different countries and regions, as well as global media issues are addressed.

This course is designed to introduce students to the theoretical and practical issues that inform international journalism and mass communication. Specifically, the course examines the different ways journalism is practiced in different cultures and explores the underlying factors that influence such practices, including technological changes that have transformed journalistic practices across the world.

course_aims: This course aims to provide students with a comprehensive and well-founded knowledge of journalistic practices andﾠmedia systems in different countries across the world. This includes the exploration of global media issues such as respect for press freedom and free speech, andﾠthe varying relationships of news media to politics and society, recognising various mechanisms of media control in different countries.ﾠThe courseﾠanalyses the impact of new technologies on journalistic practices across the world and the factors that influence foreign news coverage in various cultures, seeking toﾠbroaden students' knowledge of theﾠuse of the Internet as a research tool and as anﾠinformation resource.

learning_outcomes.description: critically examine varying systems of news media in different countries;
identify various levels of press freedom and mechanisms of media control in various countries;
understand how new technologies impact journalistic practices, especially foreign news reporting and the factors that influence the coverage of foreign events across cultures;
compare and contrast news media systems across cultures;
utilise a variety of research tools, including scholarly journals and the Internet.

assessment_details.title: Critical Analysis of Issues in International News Reporting
assessment_details.weight: 30% 900 words maximum. The maximum word limit includes in-text references and the list of references.
assessment_details.task_description: Critical Analysis of Issues in International News Reporting (30%) Assessment Task You will critically analyse an international news story published in an online newspaper in the last week of August 2026 (i.e., the story must be published sometime between 24 and 31 August 2026 ). Any news story selected outside of this timeframe will not be accepted and will not be marked. Your critical analysis must include research on the background and context of the news story, including some background information about the country on which the story is based. In terms of research, your analysis should examine factors that affect journalism practice in that country. These include but are not limited to the political, cultural, social, economic, religious, technological, legal, structural, and environmental factors. In your analysis, you should also reflect on the issues that inform international news reporting in that country, particularly the safety of journalists and their freedom to do their job without restraints. You should present convincing and logical arguments that support your assessment of these factors, using practical examples to validate your analysis. Your critical analysis should start with clear justifications for your choice of the international news story that you selected. That is, why did you choose/select that particular news story? Additionally, you should reflect on the challenges you faced while selecting the international news story, as well as the challenges you faced while analysing the story . Your reflections on the challenges you faced while selecting the news story and the challenges you faced while analysing the story should be presented in the LESSONS LEARNED section below. See the section on the STRUCTURE of the assignment. Your analysis must include the online newspaper’s link to the news story. This is to enable your tutor to verify the validity/authenticity of the story. EXCLUSIONS Magazine news reports should not be selected and should not be analysed. News reports about your own home country should not be selected and should not be analysed. That is, the news report must not relate to your own home country. News reports about Australia should not be selected and should not be analysed. These exclusions are meant to expose you to international news reporting outside of the Australian context and outside your home country environment. GUIDELINES FOR THIS ASSESSMENT LIMIT: 900 words (Maximum) . Please stick to the stipulated maximum word limit. The word limit includes in-text references and your full list of references. CRITERIA & MARKING: Assessment criteria are posted on Blackboard. REFERENCING STYLE Use the APA referencing style (7th edition). See the SS&H Library for guidelines on the APA referencing styles. APA stands for American Psychological Association. Make sure you read the Assessment Criteria on Blackboard before undertaking this assignment. Do not write in the first person. Do not use abbreviations. Ensure you proofread your assignment before you submit it. STRUCTURE OF THE ASSIGNMENT The assignment should be written like a formal essay. Please adhere to the structure outlined below by using the following subheadings to write your assignment. INTRODUCTION This section should contain a couple of opening statements to flag what you will do in the assignment. CRITICAL ANALYSIS This is where you should present your critical analysis of the international news story you selected and respond to the questions in the assignment. LESSONS LEARNED This is the section where you should reflect on the assignment in general, including the challenges you faced while considering the news story to select, as well as the challenges you experienced while analysing the news story. CONCLUSION This is where you should wrap up your argument and make a firm and definitive/concluding statement. LIST OF REFERENCES This is the section where you should list in full and in alphabetical order all the references to the literature that you cited in your assignment. Remember to use the APA referencing style (7th edition). The APA referencing style (7th edition) is available in the library. It is also in this section that you should list all the resources/works you consulted and used in your critical analysis. Only the literature, works, and resources referenced in your critical analysis should be listed in this section. PLEASE NOTE: All times listed for all assignments are Brisbane times. MARKS AND FEEDBACK: You will receive an email from the Course Coordinator to advise when your marks and feedback are ready in Gradebook. Read full task description Hide full task description

learning_activities.topic: Week 1 Lecture: Introduction to the course, the structure of lectures and tutorials, the nature of assignments and assessment criteria -- Levi Obijiofor This lecture provides you with an overview of the course, including topics that will be covered in lectures and tutorials, and a brief introduction to the assessment tasks. Powerpoint slides and audio of lectures will be available on Blackboard. Tutorial slides will also be available on Blackboard.
Week 1: NO TUTORIALS Tutorials start in Week 2. You are encouraged to engage in self-directed reading and learning this week.
Week 2 Lecture: How Australian news media report the world -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.
Week 2 Tutorial: Tutorials start this week. We will present an overview of tutorials, lectures, as well as the guidelines for assessment tasks.
Week 3 Lecture: Dangers of modern war reporting -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.
Week 3 Tutorial: NO TUTORIAL -- EKKA PUBLIC HOLIDAY No tutorial -- EKKA PUBLIC HOLIDAY. You are encouraged to engage in self-directed reading and learning.

Week 4 Lecture: Strategies of war reporting, such as "Pool System" and "Embedded Media System" of war reporting, including ethical and moral challenges of serving as an "embedded" journalist during a war -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.
Week 4 Tutorial: This tutorial will examine the question: Who is a foreign correspondent?
Week 5 Lecture: Journalists' safety, risk assessment, and strategies for surviving in a dangerous zone -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.

Week 5 Tutorial: This tutorial will discuss why risk assessment is important to freelance foreign correspondents, as well as the challenges of undertaking risk assessment in a 24-hour news environment.
Week 6 Lecture: Challenges of Reporting North and South Korea during COVID-19 pandemic . Guest Lecturer -- Dr Richard Murray
Week 6 Tutorial: This tutorial will discuss initial steps a journalist should take before taking up appointment as a foreign correspondent.

Week 7 Lecture: Special lecture to clarify the assignment -- Critical Analysis of Issues in International News Reporting -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.
Week 7 Tutorial: This week's tutorial will discuss critical issues in conflict reporting in the digital age.
Week 8: Lecture: Environmental journalism -- Guest Lecturer: Dr Kylie Navuku READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.

Week 8 Tutorial: In this tutorial, we shall discuss issues relating to cultural bias in international news reporting, drawing on Western media reportage of Africa, the Pacific, the Middle East, and other parts of the world.

Week 9 Lecture: Politics of the debate over a New World Information and Communication Order (NWICO) -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard. Read -- Levi Obijiofor’s summary of the debate: The politics of the New World Information and Communication Order. Available on Blackboard. Read -- Many Voices, One World: Towards a new more just and more efficient world information and communication order (2004). Report by the International Commission for the Study of Communication Problems. Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield. Read also: Conclusions and Recommendations, pp. 253-275. LIBRARY CALL NUMBER: HM1206 .I58 2004.
Week 9 Tutorial: This tutorial will discuss challenges that confront foreign correspondents reporting from other cultures: Their lives, times, tasks, and living conditions.
MID-SEMESTER BREAK MID-SEMESTER BREAK . You are encouraged to engage in self-directed reading and learning.

Week 10 Lecture: Guerrilla Journalism: Working as a journalist in a country under military dictatorship -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard. Read -- Olukotun, Ayo (2002). Authoritarian state, crisis of democratization and the underground media in Nigeria. Foreign Affairs , 101, pp. 317-342. Photocopy of article will be available on Blackboard. Read -- Olorunyomi, Dapo (1996). Defiant publishing in Nigeria. Media Studies Journal . Available at: http://www.lehigh.edu/~jl0d/J246-99/nigeria96.htmlGuerrilla journalism: Working as a journalist in a country under military dictatorship

Week 10 Tutorial: This week's tutorial will analyse insights presented by Isabella Higgins, ABC former Europe correspondent who also previously covered Indigenous affairs for ABC News. Isabella's insights were presented in a Reuters Institute video interview titled Putting Indigenous rights on the news agenda . The video is one hour long but we will only watch a segment of the interview and discuss issues that emerged from that interview. The video link is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mPcvPcd9oQQ . Please endeavour to watch the video and be prepared to participate in the tutorial discussion.
Week 11 Lecture: Media roles in Africa -- Levi Obijiofor READINGS Lecture slides and audio will be available on Blackboard.
Week 11 Tutorial: Growing commercialisation of journalism and its impact on professional practice. If time permits, we shall examine foreign correspondents and challenges of technology.

Week 12 Lecture: a). Teaching and Course Evaluation Survey by Students (SECaT Survey). Students will be requested to complete the Course and Teaching Evaluation Surveys (SECaT). b). Final Examination Discussion and Advice.

Week 12 Tutorial: This tutorial will discuss the uneasy relationship between foreign correspondents and senior editors in overseas head offices. The UQ Library has a helpful Communicate and collaborate online module . Email is the primary way for you to send messages to, and receive information from, the School and our staff. You must use your UQ email address (not a private address) to communicate with staff. You should add a clear subject line, including course code, and a 2-3 word statement. You can send email at any time, however, please do not expect responses outside normal working hours (Monday to Friday from ~8am to ~5pm). Emails that constitute bullying, harassment or discrimination against staff contravene the Student Code of Conduct.
